input.question: If one company buys out another company for a monetary fee, wouldn’t the money go back to the parent company, therefore the parent company essentially gained capital for free since they own the other company? How does that work?
input.ground_truth: No, because when the company is bought it is bought from its owners. You know, the shareholders? They get the money from the buyout. The only way it would stay with the company is if the company owned itself which is silly.

Question: If one company buys out another company for a monetary fee, wouldn’t the money go back to the parent company, therefore the parent company essentially gained capital for free since they own the other company? How does that work?

response.prediction:
Okay, let's imagine you have a lemonade stand (that's your first company). You do really well and make a lot of lemonade money.

Now, your big neighbor, Mr. Big, who owns a giant cookie factory (that's his company), decides he wants your lemonade stand. He gives you a bunch of cookies (that's the money he pays to buy your stand).

Now, your lemonade stand belongs to Mr. Big. But he gave you cookies for it. So, he gave away some of his cookie money to get your lemonade stand.

But here’s the thing: Now, Mr. Big gets all the lemonade money you make, too! So, he hopes that the lemonade money you make in the future will be more than the cookies he gave you.

He didn’t get the money for free. He used some of his cookie money to buy your lemonade stand. Now, he hopes that by having both the cookie factory and the lemonade stand, he will make even more money in the end.

So, when a big company buys a smaller one, they spend their own money, but they hope to make even more money later because now they own both companies. They don’t really get money for free—they spend money to get something they hope will make them more money later.
